resources.string:
Controls the final output level, stereo balance, and a transparent peak limiter that prevents digital clipping without audible artifacts.

\u2022 Output Gain \u2014 makes everything louder or quieter. Raise it if your output feels too soft; lower it if other effects are causing distortion.
\u2022 Output Pan \u2014 shifts the whole mix left or right. Useful for compensating hearing asymmetry or a lopsided room setup.
\u2022 Threshold Limit \u2014 the loudness ceiling. Lower values prevent peaks from getting too loud; if set too low, the mix will feel compressed and lose dynamics.

Automatically adjusts playback volume so that quiet and loud tracks feel balanced — no more reaching for the volume knob between songs.

\u2022 Strength \u2014 how aggressively volume is leveled. Higher values keep tracks more uniformly loud; lower values allow more natural dynamic variation between songs.
\u2022 Max Gain \u2014 how much a quiet track can be boosted. Keeps soft content from being raised so high that background noise becomes audible.
\u2022 Output Threshold \u2014 the target loudness ceiling. Lower values leave more headroom and a quieter overall output.

Normalizes loudness to a target level so every track sounds equally loud — matching streaming platform standards like −14 LUFS (Spotify) or −16 LUFS (Apple Music). Unlike simple volume control, it measures perceived loudness rather than raw peaks.

\u2022 Target LUFS \u2014 the loudness level to aim for. −14 LUFS matches most streaming services; go lower for a more dynamic, audiophile-friendly result.
\u2022 Max Gain \u2014 caps how much a quiet track can be boosted, preventing over-amplification of very quiet content.
\u2022 Speed \u2014 how quickly the adjustment reacts. Slow is smooth and gradual; Fast reacts to moment-to-moment changes but can feel pumpy on dynamic music.

Reduces the dynamic range of the signal — taming loud peaks and bringing up quieter moments — to produce a tighter, more consistent, punchier sound. Modeled on classic FET hardware compressors.

\u2022 Threshold \u2014 how loud the signal must be before compression kicks in. Lower values compress more of the music.
\u2022 Ratio \u2014 how much peaks are reduced once they exceed the threshold. Higher ratio = more squashed dynamics.
\u2022 Knee / Auto Knee \u2014 how gradually compression engages. A higher knee sounds more transparent and natural.
\u2022 Gain / Auto Gain \u2014 make-up gain to restore loudness after compression. Auto Gain handles this automatically.
\u2022 Attack \u2014 how quickly the compressor clamps down on a loud sound. Fast attack tightens transients; slow attack lets initial punch through.
\u2022 Release \u2014 how quickly it lets go after the loud moment passes. Too fast causes an audible "pumping" effect.
\u2022 Crest \u2014 balances between reacting to sharp peaks versus the average program level. Lower = snappier, more transient-sensitive; higher = smoother, denser compression.
\u2022 Adapt \u2014 lets the compressor self-adjust its timing to suit the music. Higher values = more automatic behavior.
\u2022 No Clip \u2014 prevents the output from ever exceeding 0 dBFS after make-up gain is applied.

Like a compressor, but independently applied to 3 or 5 separate frequency bands. This means a boomy bass hit won\'t cause the vocals and highs to duck — each range is controlled on its own terms, resulting in a more balanced, controlled, and detailed sound.

\u2022 Band Enabled \u2014 turns compression on or off for the selected frequency band.
\u2022 Upper Crossover \u2014 the frequency where this band ends and the next begins.
\u2022 Threshold \u2014 how loud this band must be before compression engages.
\u2022 Ratio \u2014 how strongly peaks in this band are reduced.
\u2022 Knee / Auto Knee \u2014 how smoothly compression transitions at the threshold.
\u2022 Gain / Auto Gain \u2014 make-up gain for this band after compression.
\u2022 Attack / Max Attack \u2014 how fast compression reacts in this band. Fast attack on bass tightens punch; slower on highs preserves shimmer.
\u2022 Release / Max Release \u2014 how fast compression recovers in this band.
\u2022 Crest \u2014 peak vs. program-level sensing. Lower = more transient-reactive; higher = smoother, denser.
\u2022 Adapt \u2014 allows this band\'s timing to adjust automatically to the material.
\u2022 No Clip \u2014 prevents this band from exceeding 0 dBFS after make-up gain.

Applies a correction profile (.vdc file) tailored for your specific headphone or earphone model. It compensates for the tonal colorations your headphones add — making them sound closer to a neutral, reference target.

A well-matched profile reduces listener fatigue, tightens imaging, and makes the soundstage feel more natural and monitor-like.

\u2022 Headset Correction \u2014 select the .vdc profile that matches your exact headphone model. Using the wrong profile will introduce its own coloration. Select None to bypass correction entirely.

Restores a sense of air, openness, and high-frequency detail that lossy compression (MP3, AAC) or poor recordings strip away. Rather than simply boosting the treble, it synthesizes harmonics — so the result sounds more like genuine resolution than a bright EQ lift.

\u2022 Strength \u2014 the frequency above which harmonics are generated. Lower values (e.g. 2200 Hz) add presence and body to the upper midrange; higher values (e.g. 8000+ Hz) target only the very top of the spectrum for subtle air.
\u2022 Exciter \u2014 how much synthesized content is blended in. Higher values add more sparkle and perceived detail; too high can sound harsh or artificial.

Shapes the tonal balance of the audio by boosting or cutting fixed frequency bands. It behaves like analog hardware EQ — changes affect both frequency and phase naturally, without introducing latency.

Boosting sub-bass (20–80 Hz) adds weight and rumble; cutting 200–400 Hz removes muddiness; boosting 2–5 kHz adds vocal presence; cutting 6–10 kHz tames sibilance; lifting 12+ kHz adds air.

\u2022 Band Count \u2014 more bands give finer control. 10 bands for broad shaping; 31 bands for precise surgical adjustments.
\u2022 Band Sliders \u2014 drag up to boost, down to cut each frequency region.
\u2022 Preset \u2014 a starting curve for common music genres or use cases.
\u2022 Custom Preset \u2014 save and recall your own EQ curves.

Like a surgical EQ that only activates when a specific frequency gets too loud. It leaves the sound uncolored during normal passages and only corrects problem frequencies when they misbehave — ideal for taming boomy bass, reducing harsh sibilance, or controlling nasal resonances without permanently changing the tone.

\u2022 Frequency \u2014 the target frequency to control. E.g. 100–200 Hz for boomy bass, 6–8 kHz for sibilance.
\u2022 Q Factor \u2014 how wide the band is. High Q (e.g. 5–10) = narrow surgical notch; low Q (e.g. 0.5–1) = broad musical correction.
\u2022 Filter Type \u2014 Peak affects a band around the center; Low/High Shelf affects everything below or above.
\u2022 Target Gain \u2014 how much to cut or boost when triggered. Negative = cut (most common use); positive = boost.
\u2022 Threshold \u2014 how loud the frequency must be to trigger the correction.
\u2022 Attack \u2014 how quickly the correction kicks in when triggered.
\u2022 Release \u2014 how quickly it fades out after the problem frequency settles.

Applies the acoustic character of a real space or device to the audio by loading an impulse response (IR) file. The IR captures how sound behaves in a specific environment — enabling realistic room reverb, speaker cabinet simulation, or headphone correction.

\u2022 Kernel File \u2014 the .wav impulse response to load. A room IR adds natural-sounding reverberation; a speaker or headphone IR shapes frequency response to match that device\'s character.
\u2022 Cross-Channel \u2014 blends each channel\'s processed result with the other channel. Adds diffusion and width at low values; higher values reduce stereo separation, useful when working with a mono IR.

Expands the soundstage beyond the boundaries of normal stereo, making music feel more open, spacious, and enveloping — without requiring HRTF or head-tracking. Works on both headphones and speakers.

It uses short inter-channel time delays to create a sense of depth, and at high Surround Strength settings the spatial character shifts toward a more diffuse, immersive presentation.

\u2022 Surround Strength \u2014 how wide and deep the soundstage feels. Higher values push the sound outward and create a more enveloping effect. Very high settings produce a distinctly diffuse, spacious character.
\u2022 Mid Image Strength \u2014 how prominent the center of the mix feels. Higher values bring vocals and lead instruments forward and make them feel more anchored.
\u2022 Depth \u2014 how spread-apart instruments feel laterally. Higher values push elements further apart across the stereo field.

Creates a sense of space and envelopment from standard stereo by introducing a slight time offset between the left and right channels. This mimics how the auditory system perceives sounds coming from outside and around the head, reducing the "inside-the-head" sensation of headphone listening.

\u2022 Delay \u2014 the size of the time offset between channels. Larger values (5–20 ms) produce a noticeable hall-like spaciousness; small values (1–3 ms) give subtle enhancement with minimal coloration.
\u2022 Reverse \u2014 swaps which channel receives the delay, changing the spatial direction and character of the effect.
\u2022 Wet/Dry Mix \u2014 how much of the effect is blended in. Low = subtle width; high = strong surround impression.
\u2022 LP Cutoff \u2014 rolls off high frequencies from the delayed channel to keep the spatial effect warm rather than excessively bright or diffuse. Set to 0 to disable.

Controls how wide or narrow the stereo image feels across three separate frequency ranges — bass, midrange, and treble — independently. This gives far more precise spatial shaping than a single global width control.

Keeping bass narrow makes kick drums and sub-bass feel focused and punchy; widening the highs adds air and openness; narrowing the mids tightens a diffuse, muddy mix.

\u2022 Low Width \u2014 stereo width of the bass frequencies. Below 100% narrows toward mono for tighter, more focused low-end; above 100% widens it.
\u2022 Mid Width \u2014 width of the midrange. Narrowing focuses instruments toward the center; widening spreads them across the field.
\u2022 High Width \u2014 width of the high frequencies. Widening adds air and a sense of space.
\u2022 Low Crossover \u2014 the frequency where Low and Mid bands split (default 200 Hz).
\u2022 High Crossover \u2014 the frequency where Mid and High bands split (default 4000 Hz).

Simulates the experience of listening to stereo loudspeakers in a room, on headphones. Normal headphone listening places the sound inside the head; this effect uses HRTF (head-related transfer function) processing to move the soundstage outside the head, in front of the listener — reducing listening fatigue from prolonged in-head localization.

\u2022 Quality Level (0–4) \u2014 higher levels use more detailed HRTF data for a more convincing, externalized, and room-like presentation. Level 0 is subtle and CPU-light; Level 4 is the most immersive but also most demanding. Levels 2–3 are a good balance for most devices.

Adds a sense of acoustic space to the audio — from a small, intimate room to a large concert hall. Reverb makes dry, close-mic recordings feel more natural and three-dimensional.

\u2022 Room Size \u2014 how large the simulated space feels. Larger values create longer, more spacious decay tails.
\u2022 Width \u2014 how wide the reverb tail spreads across the stereo field. Higher values feel more enveloping.
\u2022 Dampening \u2014 how much the high frequencies fade in the reverb tail. Higher values sound warmer and softer, like a carpeted room; lower values sound brighter and harder, like concrete.
\u2022 Wet Signal \u2014 level of the reverb effect. Higher = more sense of space.
\u2022 Dry Signal \u2014 level of the original unprocessed signal. Reduce for a fully ambient, washed-out effect.

Adds punch, weight, and physical impact to bass on headphones and earphones — compensating for the lack of body-conducted bass that loudspeakers naturally produce. The enhancement targets specific frequency sub-bands rather than applying a broad shelf, so the result feels tighter and more controlled than a simple bass boost.

\u2022 Dynamic Bass Strength \u2014 the overall intensity of the bass enhancement. Higher values produce stronger, more prominent impact.
\u2022 X Low / X High Freq \u2014 the frequency range that receives the primary boost. Wider settings add more warmth; narrower settings keep the enhancement focused on deep sub-bass.
\u2022 Y Low / Y High Freq \u2014 shapes how the boost energy is distributed within the bass range. Adjusting these shifts the character from deep and thumpy to warm and full.
\u2022 Side Gain Low / High \u2014 controls how wide the bass feels. Lower values keep bass mono and focused; higher values spread it across the stereo field.
\u2022 Device Preset \u2014 a starting configuration tuned for a headphone category. Adjust the X/Y/Side values to fine-tune for your specific headphones.

Makes earphones and headphones that physically cannot reproduce deep bass appear to do so. It exploits a psychoacoustic phenomenon called the "missing fundamental" — the brain perceives the pitch of a bass note even when only its upper harmonics are present, not the fundamental frequency itself.

This lets earphones with a rolloff at 70 Hz produce convincing perceived bass down to 30–40 Hz.

\u2022 Cutoff \u2014 upper limit of the bass range processed (60–150 Hz). Lower values focus only on the deepest sub-bass; higher values extend the effect into the warmer midbass.
\u2022 Intensity \u2014 how prominent the synthesized bass feels. Start around 40–60% for a natural result; too high sounds buzzy or distorted.
\u2022 Harmonic Order \u2014 which harmonics are synthesized. 2nd order is warmest and most musical; higher orders (3rd–5th) produce a stronger but more aggressive character.
\u2022 Original Bass Level \u2014 how much of the real bass signal is kept. Reducing it trades physical boom for purely perceived depth.

Boosts bass with three distinct characters to suit different preferences and headphone types. All modes blend the enhanced bass back with the original signal using soft saturation to prevent harsh peaks.

\u2022 Mode \u2014 selects the enhancement character:
- Natural Bass: smooth, full-bodied low-end boost with minimal artificial coloring. The most musical and versatile mode.
- Pure Bass+: richer and more textured, with added harmonic density. Suits headphones that sound thin or analytical.
- Subwoofer: deep, multi-resonant sub-bass impact using stacked resonant boosts. Best for music where you want to feel the bass, not just hear it.
\u2022 Frequency \u2014 how deep the enhancement reaches. Lower values (40–60 Hz) target sub-bass only; higher values (up to ~150 Hz) add warmth and body through the midbass.
\u2022 Gain \u2014 how strong the boost is. Higher values produce more prominent bass; too high introduces audible saturation.
\u2022 Fade-in (Anti-Pop) \u2014 ramps the effect in gradually on activation to prevent a loud click when toggling during playback.

The same as ViPER Bass, but sums the left and right channels within the bass band to mono before applying the enhancement. Out-of-phase bass in poorly mixed tracks causes sub-bass cancellation that weakens impact on headphones — mono summing eliminates this.

On headphones, mono sub-bass tends to feel more focused and impactful, since the brain cannot meaningfully localize deep bass from phase differences anyway.

\u2022 Mode \u2014 Natural Bass, Pure Bass+, or Subwoofer — same characters as ViPER Bass.
\u2022 Frequency \u2014 content below this is summed to mono then enhanced; content above remains in stereo.
\u2022 Gain \u2014 intensity of the bass boost.
\u2022 Fade-in (Anti-Pop) \u2014 prevents a click on activation.

Enhances perceived resolution, presence, and high-frequency detail — making music feel clearer and more articulate, especially on dull or veiled headphones.

\u2022 Mode \u2014 selects the enhancement character:
- Natural: adds subtle edge and transient sharpness without a direct treble lift. The most transparent mode; works well on headphones that are already bright.
- OZone+: a smooth, musical treble shelf centered around 8250 Hz. Like turning up the "Treble" knob on a hi-fi amplifier — adds air and brightness naturally.
- XHiFi: a more aggressive, forward-sounding enhancement that emphasizes the upper midrange and treble. Best for headphones that sound dark or veiled, or for low-bitrate audio sources.
\u2022 Gain \u2014 how pronounced the effect is. Start low and increase gradually to taste — too much of any mode can cause harshness or fatigue.

Reduces listening fatigue and the unnatural "inside-the-head" feeling of headphone listening by simulating the gentle cross-channel bleed that occurs with loudspeakers. When listening on speakers, each ear hears both channels slightly — headphones eliminate this entirely, which the brain perceives as unnatural over time.

Crossfeeding the channels back together restores a more speaker-like, frontal, and relaxed listening experience. Research consistently links crossfeed to reduced fatigue and improved frontal imaging on headphones.

\u2022 Binaural Level \u2014 the intensity of the crossfeed:
- Mild (cutoff 700 Hz, feedback 45%) — very subtle; barely narrows the stereo image, minimal change to character.
- Medium (cutoff 700 Hz, feedback 60%) — noticeably more speaker-like and frontal. A good starting point.
- Strong (cutoff 650 Hz, feedback 95%) — most speaker-like and most fatigue-reducing, but significantly narrows stereo width.

Adds the subtle warmth and harmonic richness characteristic of vintage vacuum tube amplifiers. It generates small amounts of even-order harmonic distortion — predominantly the 2nd harmonic — which the ear perceives as musical "body" and density rather than harshness.

Even-order distortion reinforces the natural harmonic series of music, making the signal feel fuller and more analog-like without sounding broken or dirty. Best used on headphones or earphones that feel overly clean or clinical.

Softens the sometimes harsh, fatiguing quality of digital audio by emulating the gentle colorations of analog circuitry — a soft high-frequency rolloff, subtle harmonic saturation, and a slight midrange coloration. The result is a warmer, more "analog" texture without sounding dull.

\u2022 Mode \u2014 how much analog coloration is applied:
- Mild: the lightest touch — barely-perceptible warmth and a very gentle treble softening.
- Medium: more noticeable warmth and analog character; reduces digital glare on bright recordings.
- Strong: pronounced bandwidth limiting and saturation; a distinctly vintage, analog sound — but significantly reduces treble response.

Applies a tuned correction filter to compensate for the tonal imbalances of the device\'s built-in speakers — their bass rolloff, midrange peaks, and uneven treble. The result is a flatter, more natural, and less fatiguing sound from the phone speaker.

Only enable this when listening through the built-in speakers. Disable it for headphones or external speakers, as the filter is tuned specifically for the internal transducers.
